title: Iluvatar Claims a Chip to Match Nvidia's H200, and the Market Punishes Everyone Paying for the Boom
subhead: Shanghai's Iluvatar CoreX says its new GPU matches Nvidia's H200 while laying out a roadmap aimed at Nvidia's Rubin, and Intel's shares fell more than 20% on a PC slowdown stretching into 2027. Meanwhile both Chinese and US AI hardware stocks are being sold on spending and margins rather than capability.

sections.heading: Iluvatar Says It Has Reached Hopper Performance, and Names Rubin as the Next Target
sections.body:
Shanghai Iluvatar CoreX said its latest GPU matches Nvidia's H200, according to the South China Morning Post, which tied the claim to China's accelerating push for a home-grown AI chip stack. Tom's Hardware reported that the newly listed company unveiled a multi-generation GPU architecture roadmap with a target of surpassing Nvidia's upcoming Rubin platform, and quoted Iluvatar's characterization as claiming Hopper-class performance today with Rubin-class performance in roughly two years.

Treat the benchmark claim as a vendor assertion, not a verified result — neither SCMP nor Tom's Hardware reported an independently run comparison. What is measurable is the surrounding context: the report lands days after Chinese regulators began allowing H200 imports for ByteDance and Tencent under case-by-case licences, according to Tom's Hardware. A domestic chipmaker claiming parity in the same month that Washington-approved H200s finally reach Chinese buyers tells you the competitive argument at home is no longer just about availability — it is about whether domestic silicon can keep enterprises from preferring imported hardware now that some imports are permitted.
sections.whyItMatters: China's AI chip story is shifting from 'can we get chips' to 'will domestic chips survive an open market.' Iluvatar's credibility now depends on customers validating the H200 comparison with real workloads, not on the roadmap slides.

sections.heading: Intel Sinks 20% as the PC Slump Outlasts the AI Boom
sections.body:
Intel shares fell more than 20% in extended trading on Thursday after the company reported third-quarter results and guided fourth-quarter revenue to $15–16 billion, below expectations, Nikkei Asia reported. Nikkei noted that the weak outlook overshadowed 21% revenue growth driven by data centers and AI.

The detail matters for industrial policy: Intel's turnaround rests on Foundry, its contract manufacturing arm, and Nikkei also reported that Intel's chief executive said the contract chip business needs 'strong' government support. Intel is the centrepiece of Washington's push to have leading-edge logic produced on US soil, so a demand collapse in its core PC business is not just an earnings problem — it weakens the balance sheet that funds a fab build-out the US government has already subsidised.
sections.whyItMatters: The AI boom is not lifting the whole semiconductor industry uniformly. Intel's legacy volume business is shrinking while its strategic mission is expanding, and its CEO is now openly stating the gap has to be covered politically.

sections.heading: The Memory Boom Is Now Inflation: Japan's Chip Export Values Jump 41%
sections.body:
Japan's exports of chip-related products rose 41% year on year in value terms in April–September, according to government data reported by Nikkei Asia, with export prices for some memory products up roughly fivefold on AI data center demand. Nikkei noted the semiconductor demand helped blunt a trade deficit pushed up by high crude prices.

A 41% export gain built largely on price rather than volume is a different signal from a capacity build-out. Memory is the part of the AI stack that trades most like a commodity, and South Korea's results this week show where the money has landed: Samsung said it became the first global technology company to post more than 100 trillion won in quarterly operating profit, per Nikkei, and SK hynix said its products are sold out until the end of the decade. Japanese equipment and materials suppliers further up the chain are collecting the same price effect.

For anyone buying AI infrastructure in Europe or elsewhere, this is the cost line that moves first: memory pricing is now a policy-relevant input to national compute plans, because sovereign AI budgets were written against 2024 price levels.
sections.whyItMatters: AI demand is being transmitted through the supply chain as price inflation. States budgeting national compute capacity are facing memory costs that have repriced by multiples, not percentages.

sections.heading: Investors Stop Paying for the Build-Out, in Both Washington and Beijing
sections.body:
The earnings week produced a coordinated reality check. Alphabet reported solid third-quarter growth and record cloud sales, but its shares fell more than 10% at one point in extended trading after it spent $51.4 billion on capex in the quarter and ended with negative free cash flow of $9 billion, according to Nikkei Asia. Google's TPUs were described as a 'meaningful' contributor to its AI business with nearly 100 customers. Separately, SCMP reported that Moore Threads, a Chinese GPU maker, saw its stock plunge despite a revenue surge, with short-term cash burn overshadowing the AI revenue story.

Nikkei also reported that Chinese AI stocks have fallen in recent weeks on similar profitability concerns, despite home-grown AI being central to Beijing's self-reliance strategy, and that Asian data center operators — including Singapore's DayOne and Australia's NextDC — are facing 'reality check' scrutiny as IPOs stall and debuts turn volatile. The common thread is not scepticism about AI capability; it is scepticism about the gap between capex and returns, in both blocs at once.
sections.whyItMatters: Capital markets are now the binding constraint on compute build-out in both the US and China. Governments that assumed private capital would carry national AI infrastructure without returns may have to fund more of it themselves.

sections.heading: Huawei's Alternative to Shrinking Transistors Gets an Update, and a Hardware Test
sections.body:
Following SCMP's report that Huawei is integrating its Tau Scaling Law design principle into next-generation wireless base stations, industry coverage (ETTelecom, summarised by Telecom Observer) fills in the underlying argument: instead of chasing smaller transistor nodes that US export controls block, Huawei is optimising for signal propagation delay (tau) using heterogenous 3D stacking and a proprietary 'LogicFolding' architecture, targeting competitive performance on 7nm or 14nm-class nodes. Huawei has claimed a 1.6x improvement in performance per watt for AI training tasks.

The commercial logic is that carrier-grade telecom gear is where Huawei has an installed base and long service relationships outside US-aligned markets, so it is the natural place to prove an architecture built under restriction. The open question is packaging: advanced 3D stacking still depends on sophisticated equipment and materials, some of which are themselves export-controlled. A design philosophy that sidesteps lithography does not automatically sidestep the toolchain.
sections.whyItMatters: If Huawei's approach holds up in deployed base stations, the argument that export controls will eventually starve Chinese telecom equipment of capability gets weaker. If packaging tools remain the bottleneck, the controls still bite — just one layer later.

sections.heading: Memory Prices Reach the Consumer Price of Chips: TSMC's 2027 Hikes and the Cost of Every AI Dollar
sections.body:
Nikkei Asia reported in July that TSMC plans to raise prices for both advanced and mature chip production by up to 10% from 2027, citing rising costs for materials, equipment and construction of overseas plants. That decision now sits inside a supply chain where memory prices have repriced by multiples and where circuit boards — a once-commoditised component — have become a bottleneck, per Nikkei's reporting on a global PCB crunch.

Two consequences follow. First, the cost of building compute is rising across almost every layer simultaneously, which makes the capital-market scepticism described above more rational than it looks: the same AI dollar buys measurably less capacity than it did a year ago. Second, mature-node price increases hit automotive, industrial and consumer electronics — the parts of the economy that have nothing to do with AI training but share the same foundries.
sections.whyItMatters: AI capex inflation is spilling into non-AI industries through mature-node pricing. The politics of that spillover, not the technology, is likely to shape 2027 subsidy debates in Europe, Japan and the US.

bottomLine: Thursday's numbers told one consistent story: AI demand is real and is now showing up as price inflation across memory, foundry services and boards, while the companies paying for the build-out are being marked down for it. Intel fell more than 20% on a PC slump, Alphabet dropped despite record cloud revenue and $51.4 billion of quarterly capex, Samsung posted the biggest quarterly profit in tech history and still saw its stock slide, and Chinese AI hardware names sold off on the same profitability question. The geopolitically relevant addition is Iluvatar's claim to H200-class performance in the same month H200 imports to China resumed under case-by-case licences — a domestic chip story that now has to survive an open market rather than a closed one. Watch two things next: whether Huawei's packaging-dependent architecture holds in deployed base stations, and whether governments respond to capex inflation by funding compute directly rather than assuming private capital will absorb it.
sources: Nikkei Asia, South China Morning Post, Tom's Hardware, ETTelecom, Telecom Observer, Reuters
